name: Aminoglutethimide (Cytadren)

lead: Aminoglutethimide (Cytadren) began as an epilepsy drug and was later used for Cushing's syndrome and hormone-sensitive cancers. Some bodybuilders have used it before contests to cut cortisol and estrogen, aiming for a leaner, drier look.

It inhibits several steroid-synthesis enzymes, notably P450scc in the adrenal gland and aromatase, lowering cortisol and estrogen. Wikipedia notes that few users report positive experiences. No trials have tested it for appearance.

paras: Medically it is an oral drug taken under supervision with corticosteroid replacement. In physique circles it has been used in short pre-contest phases, though users report it as unpleasant.

Lethargy is the most common effect; rash, low blood pressure, liver toxicity and adrenal insufficiency are reported. Medical use pairs it with corticosteroid cover. It is marketed in only a few countries.

angle.text: Aminoglutethimide blocks adrenal steroid synthesis and aromatase, and bodybuilders have used it before contests aiming to cut cortisol and estrogen for a leaner, drier look. It has been studied for Cushing's syndrome and cancer, not for physique.

lead: Aminoglutethimide is an oral nonsteroidal glutarimide, sold under names including Cytadren, Elipten and Orimeten. It was introduced in 1960 as an anticonvulsant, then found to inhibit steroid synthesis, and was later used for Cushing's syndrome, postmenopausal breast cancer and prostate cancer.[1] It was among the first adrenal steroidogenesis inhibitors and the first aromatase inhibitor used clinically.[1][2]

In bodybuilding, it has been used by some to lower cortisol and to curb estrogenic effects of anabolic steroids. Wikipedia notes that its usefulness for these purposes has been questioned, that few users report positive experiences and that risks are considered high.[1] No published trial has tested it for appearance outcomes.[3]

paras: Uses include epilepsy (petit mal), Cushing's syndrome, hormone-sensitive breast cancer in postmenopausal women and prostate cancer. It is given with a corticosteroid such as hydrocortisone to prevent adrenal insufficiency, is a second- or third-line option in breast cancer and is not effective in premenopausal women.[1] Ketoconazole produces similar hormone reductions and is described as moderately less toxic.[1]

Bodybuilders and other men have used it to lower cortisol, which is catabolic, and to inhibit aromatase to reduce effects such as gynecomastia, water retention and fat gain from anabolic steroids, often alongside an anabolic steroid to avoid androgen deficiency.[1]

Lethargy is the most frequent effect (reported in 31 to 70 percent of patients) and the most common reason for stopping. Rash and low blood pressure each occur in about 15 percent, and at least one side effect occurs in 45 to 85 percent. Other effects include nausea, dizziness, depression, weight gain and liver toxicity. Severe toxicity occurs in about 10 percent, including circulatory collapse attributed to adrenal insufficiency, and bone marrow suppression is rare.[1]

It interacts with corticosteroids, warfarin and alcohol, and is contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Labels and reviews call for monitoring of thyroid function, blood counts and liver enzymes.[1]

Aminoglutethimide is a reversible, nonselective competitive inhibitor of several steroidogenic enzymes, including aromatase, the cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme P450scc, 21-hydroxylase, 11β-hydroxylase and aldosterone synthase. Blocking P450scc suppresses adrenal steroid production, sometimes called a reversible chemical adrenalectomy. It is reported to reduce aromatase activity by 74 to 92 percent and lower estradiol by 58 to 76 percent in men and postmenopausal women, though it is considered a relatively weak aromatase inhibitor.[1] A 1978 study reported that it inhibited extraglandular estrogen production in postmenopausal women with breast cancer, and a 1967 study examined its mechanism in blocking adrenal corticosteroid synthesis.[4][5]
It is a racemic glutethimide derivative (C13H16N2O2), structurally related to glutethimide, rogletimide and thalidomide.[1]

Introduced in 1960 as an anticonvulsant, it was reported in 1963 to cause Addison-like symptoms in a young girl, a serendipitous finding that revealed steroid-synthesis inhibition. It was withdrawn in 1966 because of adverse effects, then reported in breast cancer in 1969 and prostate cancer in 1974.[1] Third-generation drugs such as letrozole were compared against it in trials.[6]
Aminoglutethimide is marketed in only a few countries, including China, Egypt and Lithuania, having formerly been sold in more than two dozen including the US, Canada and UK.[1]

Trials are in oncology and endocrinology. A randomised trial compared letrozole at two doses with aminoglutethimide in advanced breast cancer.[6] A completed phase 3 trial of tamoxifen with or without aminoglutethimide enrolled 2,021 postmenopausal women with early breast cancer, and a small phase 2 trial examined early medical adrenalectomy in prostate cancer.[7][8] Reviews trace its role as the first aromatase inhibitor.[2][3] No studies were found testing it for muscle, fat loss or other appearance goals.

timeline.event: Withdrawn from the market over adverse effects.[1]
